name: CT-RATE
description: A public open-source dataset pairing non-contrast 3D chest CT volumes with corresponding radiology text reports. CT-RATE comprises 25,692 scans from 21,304 unique patients and includes 50,188 reconstructed CT volumes. Each exam is accompanied by a report with findings and impression sections, and the dataset is enriched with 18 abnormality labels extracted from reports. The work also releases CT-CLIP and CT-CHAT built using CT-RATE.
creator: Ibrahim Ethem Hamamci
citeAs: Ibrahim Ethem Hamamci. CT-RATE: Paired chest CT volumes and radiology reports. https://huggingface.co/datasets/ibrahimhamamci/CT-RATE. 2025.
rai:dataCollection: The dataset was curated from chest CT volumes and corresponding radiology text reports from Istanbul Medipol University Mega Hospital. It includes non-contrast chest CT volumes acquired between May 2015 and January 2023, totaling 50,188 reconstructed CT volumes from 25,692 distinct CT experiments conducted on 21,304 unique patients. The authors incorporated every reconstructed volume from the hospital database, anonymized reports and metadata, translated reports from Turkish to English using the Google Translate API, and had bilingual final-year medical students review and correct all translations. Volumes involving contrast material or body parts other than the chest were excluded.
rai:dataCollectionType: Direct measurement, Secondary Data analysis, Manual Human Curator, Software Collection
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Raw data consist of chest CT volumes and corresponding radiology text reports from Istanbul Medipol University Mega Hospital. Reports were structured into clinical information, technique, findings, and impression sections. The CT-RATE dataset contains the original raw data.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Reports were anonymized by removing personal information pertaining to patients and medical professionals using targeted searches with regular expressions to identify and eliminate date-related information and patient-doctor identifiers. Reports were then translated from Turkish to English using the Google Translate API and reviewed and corrected by bilingual final-year medical students, who also removed residual personal information and ensured coherence. CT volume orientation was standardized by examining metadata, and identifying information was removed from metadata. Conditions not referenced in findings or impression were considered absent for abnormality labeling. Similar conditions were grouped under broader labels, such as left and right mucoid impactions under mucoid impaction, various lung opacities under lung opacity, and lung and fissural nodules under lung nodules.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Volumes involving contrast material or body parts other than the chest were excluded. Each volume was resized to uniform spacing of 0.75 mm in the x-axis and y-axis and 1.5 mm in the z-axis, then center-cropped or padded to a consistent resolution of 480 × 480 × 240. CT volumes were converted to Hounsfield Unit values using intercept and slope values from metadata, clipped to the range -1000 to 1000, and normalized to -1 to 1 during training. For reports, findings and impression sections were merged for label extraction. For CT-CLIP text encoding, reports with fewer than 512 tokens were padded with the <PAD> token and padded tokens were masked during attention.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Each CT exam is accompanied by a radiology report authored by a radiologist. For automated label extraction, the authors manually annotated 1,000 reports by merging findings and impression sections to create a multi-label dataset covering 18 abnormalities. The annotated reports were split into training (800) and validation (200) sets. A pretrained language model, RadBERT-RoBERTa-4m, was then finetuned on these annotations and applied to classify the remaining 24,692 reports. These classified reports were used for training the supervised baseline model, finetuning CT-CLIP, and internal evaluation. In addition, organ-level anatomical segmentation labels were generated using a state-of-the-art segmentation model and made openly available.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: The finetuned report classifier's precision, recall, and F1 scores are reported in Supplementary Table 2 and described as showing robust classification across abnormalities. Conditions not referenced in either findings or impression were considered absent. Similar conditions were grouped into broader abnormality categories before final labels were assigned.
rai:annotationsPerItem: 1 for the manually annotated subset of reports used to train the automated label extractor
rai:annotatorDemographics: Bilingual final-year medical students reviewed and corrected all report translations and examined reports for residual personal information. Three board-certified radiologists evaluated report generation outputs. Reports in the dataset were authored by radiologists.
rai:machineAnnotationTools: RadBERT-RoBERTa-4m, Google Translate API, TotalSegmentator, state-of-the-art segmentation model
rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The dataset is publicly accessible via Hugging Face. The authors state that they plan to extend CT-RATE with multi-abnormality segmentation and localization labels for 3D chest CT volumes as future work. Organ-level anatomical segmentation labels are already openly available through the CT-RATE repository on Hugging Face. No updating timeframe or deprecation policy is explicitly stated.
rai:personalSensitiveInformation: Patient age, sex, clinical information, medical history, symptoms, scan metadata, and radiology reports. The paper states that all chest CT volumes, associated metadata, and radiology text reports were anonymized before computational analysis and open-sourcing.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The paper states that the open-source release of CT-RATE, CT-CLIP, and CT-CHAT addresses critical challenges in 3D medical imaging, lays the groundwork for future innovations in medical AI, and may improve patient care. The authors also state that the models could enhance radiologists' workflows, reduce time and effort required for interpretation, and improve diagnostic accuracy in 3D medical imaging. They additionally note that the user-friendly graphical interface broadens accessibility for educational and clinical research settings.
rai:dataBiases: The authors state that biases inherent to their single-institution dataset may influence self-supervised training. Although the dataset is large and diverse, the data originate from a single geographic and clinical setting, which may limit generalizability to other populations. They also note that CT-CLIP depends on the specific terminology used in reports and the choice of prompts during zero-shot detection, and that variability in how diseases are described across radiology reports can affect detection accuracy.
rai:dataLimitations: The dataset is single-center and may have limited generalizability to other populations. CT-CLIP depends on report terminology and prompt choice during zero-shot detection. The evaluation of CT-CHAT is limited by the lack of pretrained 3D medical multimodal AI assistants for benchmarking, so comparisons are made against 2D models using DRRs and against 3D report-generation models. The quality of CT-CHAT's generated reports remains insufficient for clinical use, and the authors state that CT-CHAT is far from ready for clinical deployment. Current models are limited to chest CT volumes, and future work should extend to other modalities and anatomical regions.
rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is used for training and internal validation of CT-CLIP and CT-CHAT, for finetuning models, for zero-shot multi-abnormality detection, supervised baseline training, volume-to-volume retrieval, report-to-volume retrieval, visual question answering, and report generation. CT-RATE is divided into training and internal validation sets, with 20,000 patients allocated to training and 1,304 to validation. The authors also state that the dataset supports extensive validation and fine-tuning, and that organ-level segmentation labels may support tasks such as visual grounding and anatomical localization.
